newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's ruling leftists accept historic defeat.
newsitem.headline: Romania's ruling leftists accept historic defeat.

text.p: Romania's ruling leftist party on Tuesday conceded defeat in watershed parliamentary elections and shifted focus to the run-off presidential vote, saying Ion Iliescu had to be re-elected to ensure his country's stability.

"The voters wish is clear -- to have a government of the Convention," said Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) chief Adrian Nastase, referring to the victorious Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc led by Emil Constantinescu.
A Convention-led coalition, still to be formed, will push the PDSR out of government for the first time since the 1989 upheaval that ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

"The results for the PDSR were not very good," said Nastase. "Our choice is to enter opposition," he added, quelling suspicions the ex-communist functionaries of the PDSR would find it hard to give up power.
Nastase's remarks killed off the idea of a cross-party grand coalition, which the PDSR's Iliescu called for moments after hearing of his party's dramatic slump in the polls.
Iliescu, first in a field of 16 candidates and due to face Constantinescu in the November 17 run-off, is now certain to face a hostile parliament demanding reform should he win.

The PDSR paid the electoral price of implementing economic reform, said Nastase. But the opposition said voters had kicked out the PDSR because they had done too little to raise Romania from communist-era decay and poverty.
Nastase said Iliescu, like Russian leader Boris Yeltsin who had heart surgery in Moscow on Tuesday, was vital to foster reforms, maintain stability and ensure respect abroad.
"Yeltsin...was elected because he represents a guarantee for balanced development in Russia. It's important for Romania that President Iliescu should win the runoff," he said.

"It's important to proceed with consistent changes, but as a nation we have to know that our road is well mapped out. President Iliescu is perceived as a guarantor of Romania's international credibility in the process of NATO expansion."
The remarks implied Iliescu would campaign on the strength of his international stature rather than his domestic record.
Constantinescu, like Iliescu and third-placed Petre Roman, has disappeared from view to digest election results amid suggestions unofficial coalition bargaining has begun.

CDR officials suggested he would stick to his earlier campaign themes, attacking Iliescu for fostering corruption, neglecting the economy and blackening Romania's image by sponsoring leftist riots in the early years of his rule.
Near-complete results gave Iliescu 32 percent in the presidential poll, four points ahead of Constantinescu. Roman, whose votes are critical in the run-off, won 21 percent.
Final results were expected on Wednesday.

The Convention's most likely governing partners are Roman's Social Democrats (USD) who won 13 percent, and a party representing 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians with seven percent. The three parties are assured of a parliamentary majority.
Roman's chief of staff said the USD would give conditional backing to Constantinescu and said initial talks went well.
"If there is political will from the CDR and USD we can sign an accord by the end of this week," said Bogdan Baltazar, "The overthrow of Iliescu is vital to end the Romanian revolution."
Baltazar was referring to the anti-communist opposition charge that Iliescu manipulated the 1989 popular revolt against Ceausescu to seize power for himself. Iliescu denies this.
